clue.text: American great Andre - super server incarnate, primarily

definitions.text: American great Andre - super server incarnate, primarily

indicators.note: Primarily means in the first place, so it asks for the opening letter of each word it gathers up.

blocks.note: the opening letters of the first three words, taken in the order they stand
the opening letters of the next three, still in order

explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes the clue look like a definition on one side and wordplay on the other. It is not split at all: every word serves both jobs at once, which is what an &lit does.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is a portrait of Andre Agassi, the American tennis champion, so the sentence that spells him out also describes him.

clue.text: Harry nurtured a fringe that's brought out in summer

indicators.note: To harry is to harass and drive about, and letters driven about like that will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: fifteen letters of fodder, which is the whole enumeration

explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' reads as a name — a gardener, or the prince — and it is really a verb meaning to harass. That is the instruction, and the fifteen letters beside it are the material.
explanation.definitionFit: The tables and chairs that live outdoors, hauled out of the shed when the weather turns and put away again in autumn.

clue.text: Some characters from Lewisham blearily totter

indicators.note: Characters are letters as well as people, and only some of them are wanted, so what you need is sitting inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: Lewisham is a district of south-east London; the letters wanted run straight on across the gap between these two words, in the order they already stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blearily' looks like part of the definition — the way an unsteady walker moves — and it is only there for its letters. That is the usual shape of a hidden word: a phrase that reads like description.
explanation.definitionFit: totter → SHAMBLE: to shamble is to walk with a slow dragging gait, the unsteady progress that tottering describes.

clue.text: Everyman's description of restaurant trip - given starter of daikons - kicked off

indicators.note: A starter is what comes first at table and first in a word, so it lifts the opening letter of what follows.

blocks.note: Everyman is I, and his account of the meal reads IN IT I ATE — four words closed up into eight letters
the first letter of daikons, the long white radish

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman writes himself into his own puzzles, so 'Everyman's' is a first-person I. The word order is a poet's rather than a diner's, which is what stops the sentence sounding like wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: kicked off → INITIATED: to initiate something is to set it going, and 'kicked off' is the informal way of saying a thing was started.

clue.text: Outspoken usher

blocks.note: the blunt sense: saying the thing itself rather than working round to it
the verb an attendant does, showing somebody to a seat or pointing them down the right corridor

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, no join and no wordplay. One is an adjective about plain speaking, the other a verb about showing somebody where to go.
explanation.definitionFit: Outspoken is the frank sense, saying a thing without softening it; to usher somebody is to direct them, steering them where they should go.

clue.text: What to do to a whole (reportedly) number!?

indicators.note: Reported speech is what somebody was heard to say, so the word beside it counts for its sound and not its spelling.

blocks.note: the word for something entire is said exactly like the word for a pit in the ground, and only the second spelling is any use here
the instruction for dealing with a pit in the ground — a verb and the pronoun after it, pushed together into one five-letter word

explanation.walkthrough: Say 'whole' aloud and you have the kind you dig. What you then do to it is two words that close up into one, and the exclamation mark is Everyman enjoying himself.
explanation.definitionFit: number → DIGIT: definition by category, since a digit is a single numeral from 0 to 9 rather than any quantity you could count to.

clue.text: Rowdy: summary of journey starting in S America, ending in N America?

blocks.note: Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil, is the South American end of the trip, and a ticket prints it short
summarise any journey and it comes out as one place TO another; that joining word is all that is borrowed
the two letters an itinerary uses for the United States, at the North American end

explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes the first word look like a heading for what follows, when it is the definition standing on its own. The rest is an itinerary written the way a ticket would print it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowdy → RIOTOUS: a riotous crowd is unruly and noisy to the edge of disorder, which is what rowdy behaviour amounts to.

clue.text: It's generally understood what's possessed by Wombles

blocks.note: the plain sense: a thing everybody already knows, so nobody has to be told it
the Wombles of Elisabeth Beresford's stories live on Wimbledon Common and tidy up the litter left there, so the ground is theirs

explanation.walkthrough: The Wombles are burrowing creatures from a 1970s children's series, and the one thing everybody knows about them is where they live. Two definitions side by side, and no letters move.
explanation.definitionFit: Something everybody already knows is common knowledge; and the Wombles' patch is Wimbledon Common, so a common is what those creatures possess.

clue.text: Location of Gaol on rolling heath, as can be seen in library

indicators.note: Something rolling turns over as it goes, and a word turned over is read from its far end back to its first letter.

blocks.note: Oscar Wilde's ballad names its gaol by the Berkshire town it stood in, west of London
a heath is open moorland, and MOOR turned end for end gives these four letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaol' is the older British spelling of jail, and the prison is famous because Wilde was locked up there and wrote a ballad about it. The town's name does double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: The quiet room set aside in a library for people to sit and read, so the definition names it by where you would find one.

clue.text: Game in which you need a horse or a car

definitions.text: Game in which you need a horse

blocks.clueFragment: Game in which you need a horse
blocks.note: the mounted team game played with long mallets, four riders a side
Volkswagen's small hatchback, a common sight on European roads for fifty years

explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like it is offering a choice of equipment within one game, and it is really the seam between two definitions of the same four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The first half is the game played on horseback; the second is definition by example, one make of car happening to carry the same name.

clue.text: I ask you for victim, did you say?

indicators.note: Asking what was said moves the clue off the page and into the ear, so a different spelling of the same sound is wanted.

blocks.note: an animal hunted by another is its prey, and that word said aloud is written the other way here

explanation.walkthrough: 'I ask you' is also an exclamation of exasperation, which is how the surface wants it read. The definition needs the older sense instead, the one still alive in 'pray tell'.
explanation.definitionFit: I ask you → PRAY: the archaic sense meaning please, as in 'pray be seated' — to pray somebody is to beg or entreat them.

clue.text: Louvre: bit ugly, with too much development

indicators.note: Something ugly is misshapen, its parts not where they ought to be, and that is what has happened to the letters beside it.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, the museum's name plus the short word after the colon

explanation.walkthrough: The colon and the capital make 'Louvre' look like a topic heading, as if the clue were about the museum's glass pyramid. It is nine letters of raw material and nothing more.
explanation.definitionFit: A site with too much development on it has been overbuilt: the prefix carries the excess and the participle the building work.

clue.text: Band with grim smell

blocks.note: a band is a ring or a hoop, and a ring drawn on paper is the round letter
dour means grim and unsmiling, said of a face or a mood

explanation.walkthrough: 'Band with grim' reads as a gloomy group of musicians, which is the whole misdirection. O for a ring is worth keeping: it turns up as a band, a hoop, a duck and a love score.
explanation.definitionFit: smell → ODOUR: the formal noun for what reaches the nose, and in practice the word people reach for when the smell is not a pleasant one.

clue.text: Eccentric very loudly getting into flipping Korean exercise

indicators.note: To get into something is to end up inside it, so what stands before these words is planted within what comes after.
To flip a thing is to turn it over, and a word turned over is read starting from its last letter.

blocks.note: Tae Bo, the fitness workout built on Korean taekwondo, supplies five letters; turned round they read the other way
ff is fortissimo in a musical score, the marking that tells a player to be very loud

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a gym timetable, a long way from the definition. Keep ff: it is one of the most reliable pairs of letters in cryptics, and it is always music.
explanation.definitionFit: Eccentric → OFFBEAT: away from the regular rhythm and so out of the ordinary, the sense used of humour, films and clothes rather than of people.

clue.text: Recast, Peaky Blinders actors ultimately getting access to multiple places

indicators.note: To recast a drama is to fill its parts with different people, so the letters beside it are put into new positions.
Ultimately means at the very end, so it points at the final letter of each word it follows.

blocks.note: five of the seven letters, taken from the first word of the title
the closing letter of each of those two words, an S apiece

explanation.walkthrough: Peaky Blinders is the British drama about a Birmingham gang, and the italics mark it as a title. Only its first word is fodder; the second is there for its final letter alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A passkey opens every lock in a building rather than one, so the definition names what it gives you rather than the object itself.

clue.text: Belligerent, the writer's sent up European state cops

indicators.note: Sending a thing up lifts it, and in a down clue a lifted word is read from the bottom of the grid upwards.
To cop something is to catch or take it, so the outer pieces take the short one in between them.

blocks.note: a Pole is a native of Poland, one European among many
the writer of the puzzle is I, so 'the writer's' is I'M, and lifting it puts the two letters the other way about
Cal is the standard short form of California, a state of the USA

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends to be a news headline about European police. 'The writer' is the setter talking about himself, which is a convention worth knowing: it also comes as I, ME or the setter's own name.
explanation.definitionFit: Belligerent → POLEMICAL: given to attacking argument, the adjective for writing or speech that sets out to fight rather than to persuade.

clue.text: Sour, nasty, heartless, dead cruel

indicators.note: A nasty state of affairs is one where nothing is as it should be, and letters in that state are no longer in the order they came in.
A thing with no heart has lost its middle, and the middle of a four-letter word is the pair in the centre.

blocks.note: DEAD with its centre pair EA taken out leaves the two consonants at either end
the other five letters of the fodder, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a string of adjectives about a person, and 'dead cruel' reads as British intensifier — dead meaning very. That reading is what hides the pair of Ds.
explanation.definitionFit: Sour → CURDLED: milk that has curdled has gone sour and separated into lumps, so the two words describe one spoiled state.

clue.text: Burn arch in ruins

indicators.note: A building in ruins has its stones lying every which way, and letters left that way are no longer in the order given.

blocks.note: the fodder: four letters, the curved span of stone or brick

explanation.walkthrough: Only four letters move here, and 'in ruins' is what moves them. 'Burn arch' reads as a threat to a monument, which is the whole of the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Burn → CHAR: to scorch something until it blackens, the partial burning that leaves toast and firewood black rather than gone.

clue.text: Splash of colour desired in holy site

indicators.note: A splash of something is a small part of a larger quantity, so only a run of letters out of the phrase is wanted.

blocks.note: the letters run straight on from one word into the next, in the order they already stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Splash of colour' is such an ordinary phrase that it disappears into the surface, which is exactly what a hidden-word indicator wants to do.
explanation.definitionFit: holy site → LOURDES: the town in the French Pyrenees where a vision of the Virgin was reported in 1858, now a pilgrimage place for the sick.

clue.text: Satirise nitwit hiding electrical unit

indicators.note: Hiding a thing means keeping it out of sight inside something else, so the piece named after this word goes within the piece named before.

blocks.note: a loon is a fool, and the four letters open up to take something in
an amp is an ampere, the unit of electric current

explanation.walkthrough: 'Amp' for anything electrical is one of the standard crossword shorthands, and it is short enough to hide anywhere. The surface reads as an insult, not an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Satirise → LAMPOON: both mean attacking somebody by making public fun of them, in a cartoon, a song or a sketch.

clue.text: Nick covered in rodents: this might make you sick

indicators.note: If you are covered in something, that something is all over your outside, so the word before these two ends up within the word after.

blocks.note: the plural of mouse, and the four letters that do the covering
to nick is British slang for to steal, so a thief's verb sits under the capital letter

explanation.walkthrough: The capital N makes Nick look like a man's name, which is the trap. Rodents and a thief in one sentence buy the setter a very smooth surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A microbe is a germ too small to see, and germs are what give people infections, so the clue names the answer by what it does to you.

clue.text: Square getting verbal refusal in Rheinland

indicators.note: Verbal means by word of mouth, so the refusal is one you hear rather than one you read on a page.

blocks.note: the German for no is nein, and a German saying it produces exactly the sound an English speaker writes another way

explanation.walkthrough: The Rhineland is the German region along the Rhine, which is how the clue tells you which language to refuse in. The two words are said identically and spelt nothing alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Square → NINE: three multiplied by itself, so the definition names the class of numbers this one belongs to rather than giving a synonym.

clue.text: Take care of gold-plated cube

indicators.note: Plating is a thin coat of metal laid over the outside of something, so the metal named goes round what follows.

blocks.note: Au is gold's symbol in the periodic table, from the Latin aurum
a die is the singular of dice, the numbered cube you throw

explanation.walkthrough: 'Take care of' reads as one phrase meaning look after, and the definition stops a word earlier than you want it to. That single word is where the whole clue turns.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Take care' is what you say to somebody on parting, and adieu is the French farewell used in English for the same moment of leaving.

clue.text: Lion comes to represent Mark

indicators.note: To re-present a thing is to set it out again, and letters set out again arrive in a different order.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, both words used whole

explanation.walkthrough: The winged lion really is the emblem of St Mark, so the surface is a true sentence about Venice. The capital M is doing all the hiding.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark → SEMICOLON: a punctuation mark, and this one is the join that holds two clauses together more firmly than a comma would.

clue.text: Holy man with beam? Get lost

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for saint, printed in front of every canonised name
a beam of light is a ray, the sunshine sense rather than the timber one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Get lost' is a rude dismissal on the surface and a literal wandering underneath. St for saint is one of the first abbreviations a solver should learn.
explanation.definitionFit: Get lost → STRAY: to stray is to wander off the path and end up where you should not be, which is how a thing gets lost.

clue.text: Our dad and uncle misbehaving in the doghouse

indicators.note: Children who misbehave will not stay where they are put, and neither will the letters standing in front of the word.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder; the 'and' is joinery and contributes nothing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Misbehaving' reads as what dad and uncle are up to, which is the disguise: it is an instruction, not a description of the family.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are idioms for disgrace: someone in the doghouse is in trouble with those around them, and to be under a cloud is to be under suspicion.

clue.text: Duck leaving Rome? Yes, swimming in river

indicators.note: What leaves is gone, so the letter named just before this word comes out of the mixture before anything else happens.
Something swimming is adrift and moving about, and letters adrift like that settle into a new order.

blocks.note: seven letters to start from, before anything is taken away
a batter out for no runs in cricket has made a duck, written as a nought, and that is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: The duck is the piece of cricket the crossword borrowed: nought, and so the letter O. On the surface it is a bird flying out of Italy, which is why nobody counts the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: river → MERSEY: definition by example, since the Mersey is the river running past Liverpool into the Irish Sea and only one instance of the class.

clue.text: Looked unpleasantly flushed following return of slippery character

indicators.note: Something that returns comes back the way it went, so the word beside it is read from its far end.
Following means coming after, so the piece it belongs to takes its place behind the one the rest of the clue supplies.

blocks.note: the slippery character is an eel, and it comes back the other way round
a flushed face has gone red, so the colour is what the word is for

explanation.walkthrough: 'Slippery character' for an eel is the joke, and 'flushed' looks like embarrassment when all the clue wants from it is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Looked unpleasantly → LEERED: a leer is a sideways look full of malice or lust, so the adverb is naming which kind of look is meant.
